en: The Precious Garland / (NRa) (Vaidya 296) / Homage to the Three Jewels.
Having prostrated before the Omniscient One, the sole kinsman of all sentient beings, who is completely free from all defects and adorned with every excellence, I [shall compose this work]. (NRa 1.1)
"O King, for the sake of the arising of Dharma, I shall declare to you the Dharma that is exclusively auspicious; for Dharma attains fulfillment in one who is a vessel for the True Dharma. (NRa 1.2)
In this [treatise], first arises worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), and subsequently arises the ultimate good (*naiḥśreyasa*);
for, having attained prosperity, one proceeds step by step to the ultimate good. (NRa 1.3)
In that regard, happiness is considered worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), while liberation (*mokṣa*) is considered the supreme good (*naiḥśreyasa*).
Briefly stated, the summary of the means for this [attainment] consists of faith and wisdom. (NRa 1.4)
Through faith one practices the Dharma; through wisdom one understands it as it truly is.
Of these two, wisdom is primary, yet faith is its precursor.
He who does not transgress the Dharma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
him one should know as a person of faith, the supreme vessel for the highest good.
He who, having thoroughly examined all actions of body, speech, and mind,
and having understood what is beneficial for himself and others, always acts accordingly— he is a wise man.
Non-violence, abstention from theft, avoidance of another's wife, and restraint regarding false speech, slander, harsh words, and idle chatter. (NRa 1.8)
The complete avoidance of greed, malice, and the view of nihilism—these are the ten white paths of action; the black ones are the opposite.
Abstaining from intoxicants, a righteous livelihood, non-violence, giving with respect, honoring those worthy of honor, and loving-kindness— this, in brief, is the Dharma.
For indeed, from the mere mortification of the body there is no dharma; for therein lies neither the abstention from harming others nor the conferring of benefit upon others. (NRa 1.11)

He who, disregarding the great highway of the true Dharma— made manifest by generosity, ethical discipline, and patience— should travel by tortuous paths, subjecting his body to hardships, is like one wandering on wrong roads.
With his limbs bitten by the serpents of the afflictions, he wanders for a very long time through the terrible wilderness of saṃsāra, where infinite beings are its trees.
Through violence one is born with a short lifespan; through cruelty, one suffers many afflictions; through theft, one becomes addicted to the loss of wealth; and through adultery, one has enemies.
From lying comes rejection; from slander, the alienation of friends;
from harshness, hearing what is unpleasant; and from meaningless speech, ill fortune.
Covetousness destroys one's desires; malice is said to be the giver of fear;
wrong view is the state of false vision; and the drinking of intoxicants is the delusion of the intellect.
Through non-giving comes poverty; through a wrong livelihood, deception;
through arrogance, birth in a low family; and through envy, a lack of vital energy.
From anger comes an ugly complexion; from not questioning the wise comes stupidity.
This is the fruit in this human state, and before all of it, there is a miserable rebirth.
The ripening that has been proclaimed for these things called unwholesome,
and for all wholesome things, is the arising of results that are the opposite.
Greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the action born from them, are unwholesome;
non-greed, non-delusion, and non-hatred, as well as the action born from them, are otherwise—wholesome.
From non-virtue arise all sufferings as well as all miserable rebirths; from virtue arise all happy rebirths and all happinesses throughout every birth.
Abstention from all that is unwholesome and constant engagement in what is wholesome through mind,
action, and speech— this is remembered as the twofold Dharma.
Through this Dharma, one is liberated from the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals;
among humans and gods, one attains the full extent of happiness, prosperity, and sovereignty.
"Through the meditations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), one enjoys the bliss beginning with that of Brahmā.
Such is this Dharma of exaltation (*abhyudaya-dharma*), and this is its fruit in brief. (NRa 1.24)
Furthermore, the Dharma leading to the supreme good is subtle and profound in its vision;
it was described by the Victors as causing terror to the foolish who lack the ear [of wisdom].
"I do not exist, I shall not exist; it is not mine, it shall not be mine"—such is the terror of the fool, while for the wise man it is the destruction of fear.
"All these living beings have been described by the one who speaks solely for the welfare of creatures as being born from the notion of 'I' and accompanied by the sense of 'mine'. (NRa 1.27)
"I exist" and "mine exists"— this is false for those seeking the ultimate truth,
because through thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, neither of these two occurs.
The aggregates arise from the ego-sense; that ego-sense is unreal in reality.
For that whose seed is unreal, how can its sprout be real?
Having thus seen that the aggregates are unreal, egoism is abandoned;
and from the abandonment of egoism, there is no further arising of the aggregates.
Just as one's own reflection in the face is seen by depending upon a mirror, yet that very thing is not anything at all in reality; so it is with this.
Likewise, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is perceived by depending upon the aggregates (skandhas);
yet it does not exist in reality as anything at all, being like the reflection of one's own face.
Just as one's own reflection in a mirror is not seen without taking up the mirror, so too "I" is not perceived without taking up the aggregates. NRa 1.33.
Having heard such a teaching, the noble Ānanda attained the eye of Dharma; he himself repeatedly declared it to the monks.
As long as there is grasping at the aggregates, so long is there also the notion of "I.
When there is the ego-conception (*ahaṃkāra*), there is again karma, and from that, birth once more.
This circle of saṃsāra, consisting of three paths, is without beginning, middle, or end;
resembling a whirling firebrand, it revolves with each part serving as the cause for the other.
Because it is not apprehended as being self, other, or both, nor even across the three times, the ego-sense comes to an end; and with that, karma and birth [also cease].
Thus, perceiving the arising of cause and effect as well as their cessation,
one does not, in reality, fall into the views of non-existence or existence regarding the world.
Having heard this teaching on the destruction of all suffering, one who lacks discernment trembles due to ignorance, being terrified of that which is actually a state of fearlessness. (NRa 1.39)
All this will not exist in nirvāṇa; you have no fear of that.
Why is this non-existence, as it is being described here, so terrifying to you?
In liberation there is neither self nor aggregates; if such is liberation and you hold it dear, why is the removal of the self and the aggregates so unpleasant to you right here?
Nor is even non-existence Nirvana; how much less could it be its [or "his"] state of existence?
The exhaustion of the conceptual grasping at existence and non-existence is called Nirvana. (NRa 1.42)
In brief, the view that there is no [rebirth] and that there is no fruit of action is known as wrong view; it is non-meritorious and leads to the states of woe. (NRa 1.43)
The view that there is a self and the view that there are fruits of actions—
this is known as right view, which is meritorious and has a good rebirth as its natural result.
In that gnosis, because existence and non-existence are stilled, there is a transcendence of both sin and merit;
therefore, liberation from both miserable and happy destinies is called "blissful. (NRa 1.45)
Perceiving arising together with its cause, one transcends non-existence;
one does not resort to existence either, [perceiving] cessation together with its cause.

That which is produced prior and that which is produced simultaneously are, in reality, neither cause nor effect; for [the former] is not established through conventional designation, and [the latter] does not arise in terms of ultimate reality.
When this exists, that comes to be, just as when there is length, there is shortness;
from the arising of that, this arises, just as light arises from the arising of a lamp. (NRa 1.48)
Furthermore, in the absence of the short, the long does not exist by its own nature;
just as from the non-arising of a lamp, there is also the impossibility of light.
Thus, having seen the arising of cause and effect, one does not fall into nihilism (nāstitva),
for one has accepted this world as it truly is, born of conceptual proliferation (prapañca).

And having approached cessation—which arises from conceptual proliferation—according to reality as it is, one does not fall into the view of existence; therefore, being certain of non-duality, one is liberated.
A form seen from afar is perceived clearly by those nearby;
if a mirage were water, why would it not be seen by those nearby?
Just as this world is seen by those who have moved far away as it truly is, so it is not seen by those nearby; being signless, it is like a mirage.
Just as a mirage resembles water but is neither water nor real in its true sense,
so too the aggregates resemble a self but are neither selves nor real in their true sense.
Having come here thinking that this mirage is water, if he were to grasp it as water when it does not exist, he would indeed be a fool. (Vaidya 300) NRa 1.55
For one who grasps at this world, which resembles a mirage, thinking "it exists" or even "it does not exist," this is delusion; and as long as there is delusion, one is not liberated.
The nihilist goes to an evil rebirth, while the believer goes to a happy rebirth;
through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, one who relies on non-duality attains liberation.
One who does not desire existence or non-existence through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are—
why does such a person attain non-existence through delusion, yet not attain existence?
If, by refuting "existence," "non-existence" is implied by the force of the argument, why is it that by refuting "non-existence" alone, "existence" is not likewise implied? (NR 1.59)
Since they have no thesis, no conduct, and no mind, because they rely upon awakening—
how can those who are in fact non-existent be considered nihilists?

Ask the world— including the Sāṃkhyas, the followers of Ulūka, the Nirgranthas, and those who propound the person (pudgala) or the aggregates (skandha)— if it speaks of a transcendence of "is" and "is not."
Know that this nectar of the Buddhas' teaching, which transcends both non-existence and existence, is called "profound" because it is the dowry of the Dharma. (NRa 1.62)
It does not pass away, it does not come, nor does it even remain for a moment;
since its nature transcends the three times, how can the world exist in reality?
In reality, there is no coming, going, or staying for either of the two;
therefore, what difference could there possibly be in meaning between remaining in the world and departing from it?
Since stability does not exist, arising and cessation do not exist in reality;
how, then, could there be anything that has arisen, is stable, or has ceased in an ultimate sense?
If a non-momentary entity were always undergoing transformation, how could it exist?
If there is no transformation, from what source would there be actual change in its nature?
It might be momentary either through the destruction of one part or through total destruction;
however, because no such disparity is perceived, both of these positions are untenable.
If existence were entirely momentary, how could there be any antiquity?
And if it were non-momentary due to stability, how could there be any antiquity?
Just as there is an end to a moment, so too should its beginning and middle be conceived;
since a moment consists of these three parts, the world does not endure for even a single moment.
The beginning, middle, and end are inconceivable, like a moment; moreover,
the state of having a beginning, middle, and end arises neither from itself nor from another.
There is no single [entity], because it would have multiple spatial parts; nor is there anything without spatial parts.
Without a single [unit], there is no multiplicity, and non-existence does not exist apart from existence.
The non-existence of existence would have to arise either from its destruction or from its counteragent;
yet how could there be destruction or a counteragent, given that existence is impossible?
Therefore, the world does not suffer a loss in reality through its passing into nirvāṇa;
yet when asked whether the world is finite, the Jina remained silent.
The wise understand him to be omniscient precisely because he did not teach this profundity of the Dharma to a world that lacked the capacity for it. (NRa 1.74)
Thus, the dharma leading to the supreme good— profound, free from grasping,
and without abode— has been proclaimed by the perfectly awakened ones who perceive reality.
Because of this dharma that is without abode, people who delight in abodes and have not transcended "is" and "is not," being foolish and afraid, perish.
Those who have perished cause others to perish as well, being themselves afraid of that which lacks a source of fear;
therefore, act in such a way that you, O King, are not destroyed by those who are already lost.
Just as a plantain tree is split apart along with all its parts until nothing remains, [so should one analyze the self].
In the same way, the person is not at all split apart along with the elements.
"Therefore, the Victors have declared that 'all phenomena are without self';
and they have definitively determined that all six elements are likewise not [existent] in reality."
Neither a self nor a non-self is found according to reality;
it was for this reason that the Great Sage refuted the views concerning both self and non-self.
The Sage has declared that what is seen, heard, and so forth is neither true nor false;
for an opposing position arises from a given position, yet both of them do not exist in reality.
Thus, from the perspective of ultimate reality, this world transcends both truth and falsehood;
and for that very reason, in its true nature, it neither exists nor does not exist.
And how could an omniscient one declare that which is in every way "not thus"—
whether it be finite, or infinite, or both, or even non-dual?
Incalculable Buddhas have passed away, and likewise will there be those yet to come, as well as those present now;
from them, the end of the realm of sentient beings is considered to arise throughout the three times.
Since there is no cause for the world's increase, and its destruction occurs throughout the three times,
why did the Omniscient One leave its prior limit undeclared?
This profundity of the Dharma, which is secret from ordinary beings— the fact that the world is like an illusion— is the nectar of the Buddhas' teaching. (Vaidya 302) NRa_2.9 //
Just as the birth and end of an illusory elephant may be perceived, yet neither its birth nor its end exists in reality; so it is with all things.
For this world, which is like an illusion, birth and likewise death are perceived; yet in the ultimate sense, neither birth nor death exists at all.
Just as a magical elephant comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, it does not abide as a real entity because it is merely a delusion of the mind. (NRa 2.12)
Likewise, the world is like an illusion; it neither comes nor goes anywhere, and because it is merely a delusion of the mind and lacks intrinsic existence, it does not abide.

What entity in reality could there be—whether it exists, does not exist, or even might exist—who transcends the three times? Such a thing is the world itself, except as a matter of conventional usage.
Because it is of four kinds—namely, as peaceful, infinite, dual, and non-dual—the Buddha declared this [universe] to be indeterminate for no other reason. (NRa 2.15)
The impurity of the body is, for its part, gross and within the range of direct perception;
yet, even though it is constantly seen, when the mind does not remain [fixed upon it], [what can be done]? (NRa 2.16)
How can this True Dharma—so exceedingly subtle, profound, and without abode—be easily entered into the mind when it is not directly perceived? (NRa 2.17)
Having awakened, the Sage turned away from teaching the Dharma to us,
realizing that this Dharma is difficult for people to understand due to its extreme profundity.
This Dharma, if poorly understood, destroys the person lacking wisdom, because he sinks into the impurity of the view of non-existence. (NRa 2.19)
Moreover, another fool who, due to his failure to understand this, fancies himself a scholar,
perishes by rejecting it and goes headfirst down to the Avīci hell.
Just as one meets with destruction through food that is poorly consumed,
so too one attains long life, health, strength, and happiness through food that is well consumed.
Thus, through a misunderstanding of this [teaching], one meets with destruction;
but through its correct understanding, one attains happiness and unsurpassed awakening in this very life. (NRa 2.22)
Therefore, having abandoned here both the view of repudiation and the nihilistic view, exert yourself toward right knowledge for the sake of accomplishing all goals. (NRa 2.23)
Due to the lack of full understanding of this Dharma, egoism persists;
from that arises wholesome and unwholesome karma, and from that, wholesome and unwholesome birth.
Therefore, as long as the Dharma that destroys the sense of "I" remains unknown,
remain devoted to the practices of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience. (NRa 2.25)
O King, one who accomplishes tasks that have dharma as their beginning, dharma as their middle, and are rooted in dharma, does not suffer in this world nor in the next. (NRa_2.26)
From dharma come fame and happiness; there is no fear here for one who dies having practiced it, and there is abundant happiness in the next world. Therefore, always devote yourself to dharma.
Dharma alone is the supreme policy; through Dharma the world is won over.
For when the world is won over, one is not deceived either in this world or in the next.
But by a policy based on unrighteousness, the world becomes alienated;
and through the alienation of the world, one finds no joy neither in this world nor in the next.
Devoted to deceiving others, this miserable path to the lower realms is a science of misfortune;
how has it been turned by those of poor wisdom into a science of profit? (NRa 2.30)
How can one who is intent on deceiving others be considered wise in terms of true purpose, by which very act he deceives himself for many thousands of births? (NRa 2.31)
Seeking to cause displeasure to an enemy, abandon faults and resort to virtues;
for in this way, while achieving your own welfare, you will also bring about what is unpleasant for the enemy.
Through generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and consistency between words and deeds—
with these, practice the gathering of the world and of the Dharma itself.
Just as truth alone generates firm confidence in kings,
so too does even untruth produce the utmost lack of trust in them.
Truth is not that which is non-contradictory; rather, truth is that which is elevated in meaning for the sake of sentient beings.
That which is exclusively beneficial to others is truth, while the other is falsehood because it is harmful.
Just as a brilliant display of generosity on the part of kings conceals their faults,
so too does their miserliness destroy the entirety of their virtues.
For one who is tranquil there is profundity; from profundity comes supreme dignity; from dignity come splendor and authoritative command; therefore, devote yourself to tranquility.
Because his intellect is unassailable due to his wisdom, he is independent of others and steadfast;
thus a king is not deceived. Therefore, be devoted to wisdom.
A king who possesses truth, generosity, tranquility, and wisdom is praised by gods and humans as one who is "fourfold auspicious," just like the Dharma itself which is likewise fourfold auspicious.
For one who constantly sits together with those who speak with restraint, who are pure, and who are stainless through wisdom and compassion, wisdom and the Dharma increase.
Those who speak what is beneficial are rare; those who listen are even rarer;
but those who act quickly upon what is beneficial are the rarest of all. (NRa_2.41)
Therefore, knowing that what is beneficial may be unpleasant, practice it immediately;
just as a self-possessed person drinks even a potent medicine for the sake of health.
Always contemplate the impermanence of life, health, and sovereignty; then, filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, you will devote yourself exclusively to the Dharma.
Seeing that death is inevitable and that there is suffering for one who has died due to evil deeds,
you ought not to commit sin even for the sake of worldly pleasure.
If fear has been seen in one thing and fear has been seen at some moment in another, and if you find consolation in one, why do you not feel fear in the other? (NRa 2.45)
From liquor comes contempt in the world, the ruin of one's duties, and the loss of wealth;
through delusion, one performs what should not be done—therefore, always renounce liquor.
[NRa_2.46] ... (The Sanskrit text for 2.47–95 and 3 is lost) 4.
Since kings are generally praised even when practicing unrighteousness that ought to be followed by their dependents, they find it difficult to distinguish between what is endurable and what is not.
If even anyone else at all should endure unpleasant words that are difficult to speak,
how much more so you, a king ruling over the great earth, when addressed by me who am but a mendicant?
But solely out of affection for you and out of compassion for the worlds,
I alone speak to you words that are extremely beneficial, even though they are unpleasant.

"The disciple should be addressed at the proper time with words that are truthful, gentle, meaningful, and beneficial, out of compassion"—thus the Blessed One has said; therefore, you are being addressed in this manner.
If, while remaining established in freedom from anger and truthful speech, one is praised,
one should accept that praise as one would accept pure water for the purpose of bathing.
Having understood that these words I speak are beneficial for you both in this world and the next, act accordingly for your own welfare and for that of the world as well.
If, having previously obtained wealth from supplicants, you do not give it away,
you will not obtain wealth again due to both ingratitude and greed.
In this world, a porter who is not paid does not carry the provisions; however, in the next world, the beggar who was not supported here becomes a carrier of a hundredfold more.
One whose mind is always noble and who delights in noble deeds—
every fruit born of such noble action is itself noble.
Establish a glorious and renowned seat of Dharma— a sanctuary for the Three Jewels— that has never even been touched by the feeble desires of worldly kings. (Vaidya 305) NRa_4.10 //

O King, that which does not cause the hair on the bodies of neighboring kings to stand on end and which is not a foundation for the Dharma is better left undone; for even after death, it remains unrecommended.
By means of extreme magnificence, cause the noble to increase their wonder and enthusiasm, and cause the dull-witted to feel inspired—even at the cost of your entire possessions. (NRa 4.12)
Having been forced to abandon all your possessions, you must depart for the next world;
yet that which has been dedicated to the Dharma goes before you, as does everything else.
Has the entire property of the former king come under the control of this king for the sake of the former one’s merit, happiness, or even fame? (NRa_4.14)
From wealth enjoyed here comes happiness; from wealth given away, happiness in the next world.
But since that which is neither enjoyed nor given away is lost, there is only suffering—how could there be happiness?

As you are perishing, you will not be able to give [the kingdom] away because of your lack of independence, owing to ministers who are intent on severing calamities, devoid of affection, and seeking to please the new king.
Therefore, remaining composed even at the cost of all your possessions, quickly establish yourself in the foundation of Dharma;
for you stand amidst the conditions of death like a lamp in a gale.
Furthermore, whatever other matters pertaining to the Dharma were previously established by former kings,
such as the maintenance of temples for the gods and so forth, let those also be carried out exactly as they were.
They should be served by those who are non-violent, of virtuous conduct, established in their vows, fond of guests, all-forgiving, free from quarrels, and ever-diligent.
The blind, the diseased, the maimed, the wretched, the helpless, and the beggars—
these too shall receive food and drink with impartiality, without obstruction.
Even for those who are without wealth, if they are righteous,
extend appropriate favors, even if they reside in the territories of other kings.
In all matters concerning the administration of justice, appoint a judicial officer who is upright, free from greed, wise, and righteous; ensure that he does not cause harm to them.
Appoint as ministers those who are knowledgeable in policy, righteous, affectionate, pure, devoted, undaunted, of noble birth, endowed with good character, and grateful.
Appoint as commanders of the army those who are noble, generous, brave, affectionate, capable of sharing in prosperity, steadfast, ever-vigilant, and righteous.

Appoint as officials those who are virtuous in character, pure, capable, knowledgeable of practical affairs, experts in the treatises, established in their livelihoods, impartial, affectionate, and mature.
"And every month, you must hear from them the full account of income and expenditure;
having heard it, you yourself shall first address all matters pertaining to the administration of justice. (NRa_4.26)
If your kingdom is for the sake of Dharma, and not for the sake of fame or sensual pleasure, then it is exceedingly fruitful; otherwise, it is for the sake of misfortune.
O King, in this world where people for the most part have become prey to one another,
listen to how you may ensure both your sovereignty and your righteousness.
May many elders in wisdom, born of noble lineage, knowledgeable in justice, and fearful of sin, always assemble together to oversee your affairs.
Even if they should inflict punishments, imprisonment, or blows according to the law,
you should always remain moist with compassion and be full of grace toward them.
O King, out of compassion, you should constantly uplift the minds of all embodied beings for their very welfare, even those who commit grave evils.
Compassion should especially be exercised toward those who commit violent and grave sins;
for it is precisely such self-destructive individuals who are the objects of compassion for the great-souled ones.
Every day, or every five nights, release those who are bound and exhausted;
release the rest as well according to what is appropriate, but do not fail to release anyone at all.
In those toward whom the thought of not liberating them arises, non-restraint (asaṃvara) is born;
from that non-restraint, evil is accumulated incessantly.
And as long as they are not liberated, let them remain bound in happiness, provided with hair-cutting, bathing, drink, food, medicine, and clothing. (NRa 4.35)

Just as one might strike unworthy sons out of a desire to make them worthy recipients, so too should physical correction be administered out of compassion, and not out of hatred or a desire for material gain.
Having reflected thoroughly and having correctly identified those who are wicked and even murderers,
deprive such men of their territory without killing them or causing them physical pain.
Behold all things and every object with the eye of your spies;
being ever vigilant and mindful, perform your duties in accordance with righteousness.
Constantly honor those established in virtue with gifts, respect, and hospitality;
likewise, according to the rules, honor the rest as well with noble and appropriate treatment.
The royal tree— its abundant flowers being honor, its great fruit being gifts, and its shade being forbearance— is resorted to by the birds that are his servants.
A king who possesses the virtue of renunciation becomes radiant and beloved,
just as a sugar-candy is made delicious even when roughened with cardamom and black pepper.
And for you, the "law of the fish" shall not prevail; thus, your kingdom will be governed by justice.
Therein shall be neither injustice nor unrighteousness, but rather righteousness itself.
You did not bring this kingdom from the next world, nor will you take it with you;
since it was obtained through righteousness (*dharma*), you ought not to commit unrighteousness (*adharma*) for its sake.
O King, let such an effort be made that you do not acquire, by means of the kingdom as the price for merchandise, a continuous succession of the wares of suffering. (NRa_4.44)
O King, let such an effort be made that you may enjoy the succession of royal treasures by means of the kingdom as their price.
Even for a universal monarch who has obtained the earth with its four continents, only these two kinds of happiness are recognized: that of the body and that of the mind. (NRa 4.46)
Bodily pleasure is merely the counteraction of suffering; mental pleasure, however, consists solely of perception and is produced by conceptual construction. (NRa 4.47)

The entire essence of happiness for the world is merely the counteraction of suffering and nothing more than a mental construction; therefore, it is devoid of reality from the perspective of ultimate meaning.
The enjoyment of islands, countries, cities, dwellings, regions, and locations, as well as beds, food, drink, elephants, horses, and women, belongs to each individual alone. (NRa 4.49)
And when the mind is present where it should be, then indeed there is happiness;
for the others, due to the absence of mental attention (*amanaskāra*), they are in fact rendered useless.
If one does not conceptualize the five objects by means of the five sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, while perceiving them, then there is no pleasure therein. (NRa 4.51)
Whichever object it cognizes by whichever sense-faculty, at that time the remaining [faculties] do not perceive the remaining [objects], because they would then be entirely useless. (NRa 4.52)
Having perceived the form of an object previously apprehended by the senses, the mind, as it conceptualizes that which has passed away, imagines it to be pleasure. (NRa 4.53)
Even though a single sense-faculty perceives a single object here [in this world], that faculty is useless without its object, and the object is likewise useless without it. (NRa 4.54)
Just as the birth of a son is said to occur in dependence upon the mother and father,
so too is the arising of consciousness said to occur in dependence upon the eye and visible form.
Past and future objects, along with the sense faculties, are useless;
and those which are present are also useless, because they do not exceed that pair [of past and future]. (NRa 4.56)
Just as the eye perceives a circle of fire due to a visual error,
so too do the sense faculties perceive objects as if they were present.
The sense faculties and the objects of the sense faculties are considered to be composed of the five elements;
since each individual element is devoid of intrinsic reality, these [faculties and objects] are in fact devoid of reality.
If there were a separation [of elements] among beings, it would follow that fire exists without fuel;
if there were a conjunction, there would be an absence of defining characteristics. This same conclusion applies to the remaining [elements] as well.
Thus, since both [types of] beings are purposeless, their association is in vain;
and because association is thus purposeless, form is therefore purposeless in reality.
And for consciousness, feeling, perception, and mental formations, in every respect, the self is individually useless; from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is utterly devoid of purpose.
Just as the conceit of happiness regarding the remedy for suffering is [merely] a designation according to the facts,
so too the conceit of happiness regarding actual happiness is born from the obstruction [of suffering].

Thus, through the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*), craving for union with pleasure and craving for separation from suffering are abandoned; therefore, liberation belongs to those who perceive this. (NRa 4.63)
If it is asked, "What is it that sees?", it is conventionally said to be the mind (*citta*).
For a mind without mental factors (*caitta*) is not accepted, as it would be purposeless.
Having thus understood the world to be in vain according to its true nature, one becomes supportless;
like a fire without fuel, one attains nirvana, being without any substratum for rebirth.
The Bodhisattva also, having seen this, is considered destined for perfect enlightenment;
however, out of compassion alone, his continuity of existence persists until awakening.
The equipment of a bodhisattva has been taught by the Tathāgatas in the Mahāyāna; yet it is reviled by those who are both deluded and hostile.
Either one who is ignorant of virtues and faults, or one who perceives faults in what is virtuous, or even one who hates virtue and reviles the Mahāyāna. // NRa_4.68 //
Having understood that faults harm others while virtues benefit others, one who hates virtue is said to be a reviler of the Mahāyāna.

Because it is indifferent to its own self-interest and delights solely in the singular flavor of the welfare of others, that Great Vehicle is a mine of virtues; therefore, he who hates it is consumed by that very hatred.
Even a faithful person may become hostile through a misconception, or another may become so out of anger;
even a faithful person is said to be "burnt," so what need is there to mention one who is hostile by nature?
Just as physicians have stated that one poison may be used to destroy another poison,
what contradiction is there in saying that even through suffering one may destroy what is harmful?

Since it is taught in the scriptures that "all phenomena are preceded by the mind and the mind is supreme," how could one who is intent on what is beneficial perform what is harmful even through suffering? (NRa 4.73)
Even that which is painful should be performed if it is beneficial for the future; how much more so that which is pleasant and wholesome?
This is the eternal law for oneself and for others.
If, by relinquishing a small pleasure, a vast happiness is to follow later, the wise person should abandon that small pleasure, perceiving the vast happiness. (NRa 4.75)
And if this [suffering] were not felt by those who administer bitter medicine, then physicians and the like would be destroyed; yet this is not logical.
Even that which appears to be indolent is sometimes seen by the wise as beneficial;
for both the general rule and its exception are praised in all treatises.
In that Mahāyāna where all outflows are preceded by compassion and are stainless with wisdom, what person possessing consciousness would revile it?
Because of its extreme vastness and profundity, the Mahāyāna is today reviled out of delusion by those of undisciplined mind who are despondent and act as enemies to themselves and others.
Since the Mahāyāna consists of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and compassion, how could there be any ill-spoken word within it?
The benefit of others is accomplished through generosity and ethical discipline; one’s own [benefit] through patience and vigor;
and meditation and wisdom lead to liberation—this is the summary of the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
In brief, the Buddha’s teaching consists of the welfare and liberation of oneself and others;
since these have the six perfections as their core, this word of the Buddha is such.
Wherein the Great Path to Awakening, consisting of merit and knowledge, was taught by the Buddhas—that is the Mahāyāna; indeed, it is not seen due to ignorance.
Because his qualities are inconceivable, the Jina is said to possess "inconceivable qualities";
therefore, let this greatness of the Buddha in the Mahāyāna be accepted.
Since even the noble Śāradvatīputra’s range does not extend to the mere quality of [the Buddha’s] ethical discipline,
why is that inconceivable majesty of the Buddha not tolerated?
In the Mahāyāna, non-arising is [the meaning of] emptiness, whereas for others it is exhaustion;
since exhaustion and non-arising are identical in their actual meaning, let this be accepted.
For those who thus perceive emptiness and the majesty of the Buddha through reasoning,
how could the teachings spoken in the Mahāyāna and elsewhere not be consistent for the wise?

Because it is difficult to understand the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*), one should protect oneself through equanimity regarding the statements concerning the single vehicle and the three vehicles.
For through equanimity there is no demerit; from hatred comes evil—how then could there be virtue? Therefore, those who desire their own welfare ought not to harbor hatred toward the Mahāyāna.
Neither the vow of a bodhisattva nor the dedication of practice is taught in the Śrāvaka vehicle; therefore, how could one become a bodhisattva from that? (NRa 4.90)
The foundations for a bodhisattva’s awakening have not been taught by the Buddhas, nor is there any other authority; who in this matter is superior to the Conquerors?
Since the path associated with the bases, the noble truths,
and the factors of enlightenment is common to the disciples, by what means is the fruit of a Buddha superior?
The words spoken in the sūtras for the purpose of establishing the conduct of awakening were not fully expressed;
they have been fully expressed in the Mahāyāna, and therefore they should be accepted by the wise.
Just as a grammarian would teach even the alphabet,
so did the Buddha teach the Dharma to those to be trained according to their capacity.
To some he taught the Dharma for the sake of turning away from evil;
to some for the sake of accomplishing merit; and to some that which relies upon both.
For some, it is independent of the two extremes; for others, it is profound and terrifying to the fearful;
for yet others, it is the means of achieving awakening, with emptiness and compassion as its core.
Thus, the virtuous should eliminate all resentment toward the Mahāyāna;
rather, they should cultivate even greater faith for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment.
Through faith in the Mahāyāna and by practicing what it teaches,
unsurpassed awakening is attained, as well as all forms of happiness in the interim.
Generosity, ethical conduct, patience, and truthfulness—these, especially for the householder, are said to be the Dharma whose essence is compassion; let this be firmly internalized.
Moreover, because it is contrary to the ways of the world, ruling a kingdom according to Dharma is difficult;
therefore, for the sake of Dharma and fame, your attainment of the life of renunciation is appropriate.
In the *Ratnāvalī*, the fourth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Conduct of Kings."
